text: Walk through almost any new part of a city and something feels strangely familiar.
The cars arrive in the same narrow palette.
The cafés share pale wood, black metal, and green.
Logos use clean letters. New apartment blocks repeat grids of glass, concrete, and muted cladding.
It can feel as if all of it came from one invisible catalog.
But the world does not literally look the same.
Tokyo is not Lagos. Geneva is not Mexico City.
A family shop is not a global franchise.
The past was never one continuous carnival of color.
This is not a film about a secret committee that deleted personality.
Different industries, facing different problems, have begun solving them with the same visual vocabulary.

That distinction—between being loved and avoiding rejection—appears far beyond cars.
Psychologists call this processing fluency: the ease of making sense of something.
Research suggests familiar forms, clear contrast, and repeated exposure can be easier to process, and that ease can influence preference.
This does not mean simple is objectively beautiful.
Complexity can create interest, identity, and meaning. Familiarity can also become boredom.
But in a crowded marketplace, immediate comprehension has value.
A product has seconds to explain itself on a shelf.
A building proposal must survive clients, planners, engineers, budgets, and neighbors.
A brand must remain recognizable on a billboard and inside a tiny icon.
At every stage, unfamiliarity creates a question. A question creates friction.
And friction needs someone willing to defend it.
Nowhere is low friction more visible than on a screen.
Jakob Nielsen summarized a basic rule of internet behavior: users spend most of their time on other websites, so they prefer a new site to work like the sites they already know.
That is good usability. A shopping basket should not become a puzzle.
Navigation should not demand a tutorial. Familiar patterns make digital services faster and more accessible.
But successful conventions spread beyond function. The same rounded cards.
The same generous white space. The same centered headline.
The same soft gradient. The same friendly geometric type.
Logos face a related pressure. They must remain clear across phones, watches, browser tabs, packaging, video, and physical signs.
Responsive identity systems often remove detail as space becomes smaller.
Each individual simplification may be rational. The convergence appears one decision later—when every company reaches for the same solution to signal that it is modern, trustworthy, and easy to use.
Physical space follows a similar logic. Early McDonald’s restaurants were designed to attract attention.
The company’s own history describes the red-and-white tiled building, created in 1953, as an attention-getting design.
The arches were not merely a logo placed on the building.
They were part of the building. In the late nineteen-sixties, that design gave way to the Mansard roof, which could be repeated and remodeled across a growing system.
The lesson is not that every chain became a gray box.
McDonald’s itself highlights contemporary locations that use existing architecture and distinctive local features.
The lesson is that scale changes what a design must do.
A one-off building can be inseparable from its site.
A repeatable system must adapt to different plots, regulations, contractors, climates, maintenance schedules, and customer expectations.
The larger the network, the more valuable the adaptable container becomes.
Identity then migrates into controlled layers: signage, furniture, packaging, lighting, menu screens, and the app.
The building becomes quieter so the system can travel further.
At this point, sameness can emerge without anyone choosing sameness as the goal.
One developer copies a layout that sold quickly.
One designer chooses a familiar typeface. One café recreates a photogenic interior.
One platform recommends work similar to what held attention.
Different actors can reinforce the same pattern without coordinating.
No single choice transforms culture. Each becomes evidence for the next.
Recommendation systems make this tension explicit. Spotify researchers describe balancing familiarity and similarity against discovery.
The platform does not simply maximize sameness; it manages competing objectives.

Algorithms did not invent visual convergence. They can accelerate a loop that already exists: what is familiar is easier to recognize; what is easier to recognize is easier to choose; what is chosen becomes easier to measure; and what is measured becomes easier to imitate.
This loop is our model, not Spotify's finding.
The conspiracy is not a room full of designers agreeing to make everything identical.
It is a feedback loop in which nobody wants to be the expensive exception.
But a useful theory must explain its limits.
If scale automatically destroyed difference, every global brand would look identical in every city.
They do not. If digital legibility required one style, every successful interface would use the same colors and shapes.
They do not. If neutral cars were the inevitable result of economics, expressive models would never sell in bright colors.
They do. Constraints narrow possibilities. They do not eliminate choice.
And once a visual language becomes too common, difference can recover economic value.
A colorful car becomes memorable because the road is neutral.
An ornate wordmark stands out because competitors use plain type.
A restaurant filled with local materials becomes a destination because the standardized alternative is everywhere.
This is why design moves in cycles. A solution spreads because it works.
It becomes a convention because it is copied.
Then the convention creates an opportunity for someone willing to break it.
Sameness contains the conditions for its own reversal.
So why does everything look the same now?
Not because everything is the same. Because across the cases we have seen, design happens inside systems that reward legibility, familiarity, adaptability, and measurable performance.
Those pressures are real. They can help products function, interfaces remain usable, buildings get approved, and brands operate at scale.
The problem begins when a useful constraint is mistaken for an aesthetic commandment.

When “easy to recognize” becomes “must look familiar.” When “adaptable” becomes “without local character.” When “low risk” becomes “without a point of view.” The world does not have to become identical for difference to become harder to defend.
And perhaps that is the hidden cost of frictionless design.
We notice fewer bad surprises—but also fewer good ones.
Personality requires an argument. It may cost more, divide opinion, age badly, or fail.
Many distinctive things began as choices that could not be defended by saying: everyone else is doing it.
Sameness is rarely imposed all at once. It accumulates, one reasonable decision at a time.
And difference returns the same way: one defensible exception at a time.
